NavBridge is the phone half of a two-part navigation system. The other half is an ESP32-S3 dashboard mounted on the vehicle, which draws the map, the route and the turn arrows. This app gives that dashboard the three things it cannot get on its own: a position, a route, and an address search.

WHAT IT DOES

Position. Android’s fused location provider (the same one the phone’s own maps app uses — it blends GNSS with Wi-Fi and cell positioning) is polled about once a second. Each fix is converted to standard NMEA sentences and sent over UDP to the dashboard, which parses them exactly as it would a wired GPS module. This runs as a foreground service so Android keeps it alive with the screen off.

Routing. When you tap a point on the dashboard and press GO, it sends a request over UDP to this app, which asks the separately installed BRouter app to compute the route offline, then streams the polyline and the turn instructions back in small chunks. Nothing about routing needs an internet connection.

Address search. The magnifier on the dashboard sends the typed text here, and this app queries the public Photon geocoder, biased toward your current position so a nearby match wins over an identically named place abroad. This is the one feature that does need internet.

Turn guidance. The dashboard tells this app when a turn is coming, and the app speaks it and vibrates. The decision is made on the dashboard rather than recomputed here, so what you hear can never disagree with the arrow you are looking at.

WHAT YOU ALSO NEED

BRouter, by abrensch. Free and open source, on F-Droid and Google Play. Install it, open it once, and download the offline routing data for your region — without that, GO on the dashboard returns an error. NavBridge talks to it through its published service interface; BRouter never has to be in the foreground.

The dashboard firmware, flashed to an ESP32-S3 display board. It also wants a microSD card: map tiles are cached there, and that cache is what lets the map keep working once you ride out of phone coverage.

A shared network. Phone and board must be on the same Wi-Fi — in practice the phone’s hotspot, with the board joining it. The IP on the main screen is the board’s address on that network.

Map imagery comes from OpenStreetMap and is cached on the board’s SD card; routing data and geocoding are OpenStreetMap-derived as well. © OpenStreetMap contributors.

PRIVACY

Your position goes to two places: the dashboard on your own network, and — only while you are actively using address search — the Photon geocoder, as a bias for the query. Nothing is logged, stored or sent anywhere else. Routing never leaves the phone.
